The phalanges of the big toe (hallux) are thick and strong; they are the last point through which weight passes in the push-off phase of walking.
clinical: Hammer toe deformity and gouty arthritis (especially of the 1st MTP joint – podagra) are common problems.
tus: Hallux valgus is lateral deviation of the big toe; a bunion develops over the head of the 1st metatarsal.

entries.summary: The adult human skeleton consists of about 206 bones and has two main divisions: the axial skeleton, forming the central axis of the body (skull, vertebral column, thoracic cage), and the appendicular skeleton, which carries the arms and legs (girdles and the bones of the free limbs).
facts: About 206 bones in the adult; around 270–300 in the newborn, counting the parts not yet fused
80 bones: skull and ear ossicles (29, including the hyoid), vertebral column (26), thoracic cage (25: sternum and 24 ribs)
126 bones: shoulder girdle (4), upper limbs (60), pelvic girdle (2), lower limbs (60)
Long (femur, humerus), short (carpal bones), flat (sternum, skull vault), irregular (vertebrae), pneumatic (maxilla, ethmoid) and sesamoid (patella) bones
Support and shape, protection of organs, levers for movement, blood formation (red bone marrow), store of calcium and phosphate
sections: Girdles

The shoulder girdle consists of the clavicle and scapula; it is attached to the trunk only by the sternoclavicular joint and allows a wide range of movement. The pelvic girdle consists of the two hip bones; joined firmly to the sacrum behind and to each other in front, it transmits the body weight to the legs.
clinical: In adults, bone marrow biopsy and aspiration are usually taken from the posterior iliac crest (around the posterior superior iliac spine).
Bone age is assessed from the ossification centres on an X-ray of the left hand and wrist.
tus: The axial skeleton has 80 bones, the appendicular skeleton 126.
In adults red bone marrow is found mainly in the flat bones (sternum, ribs, hip bone, vertebrae) and the proximal ends of long bones.

entries.summary: Bone is a hard connective tissue made of calcium phosphate crystals and collagen. Dense compact bone lies outside and spongy bone inside; the surface is covered by periosteum. Bones develop by intramembranous or endochondral ossification.
facts: Compact (cortical) bone – made of osteons (Haversian systems); spongy (trabecular) bone – bone marrow lies between the trabeculae
Osteoblast (builds bone), osteocyte (mature cell embedded in bone), osteoclast (resorbs bone; multinucleated cell of monocyte origin)
Epiphysis (end), metaphysis (transition zone where growth takes place), diaphysis (shaft, containing the medullary cavity), epiphyseal plate (growth cartilage)
Intramembranous: skull vault, facial bones, most of the clavicle. Endochondral: skull base, vertebrae, most limb bones
The diaphysis is supplied by the nutrient artery (entering at the nutrient foramen), the ends by metaphyseal and epiphyseal arteries, the outer cortex by periosteal arteries
sections: Periosteum and endosteum

The periosteum is a membrane rich in nerves and vessels covering the outer surface of bone; cells of its inner layer allow the bone to thicken and fractures to heal. There is no periosteum on joint surfaces, which are covered by hyaline cartilage. The endosteum lines the marrow cavity.
Growth

Long bones grow in length as cartilage cells in the epiphyseal plate multiply and ossify; the plate closes at the end of puberty (leaving the epiphyseal line). Growth in width occurs as the periosteum adds new bone.
clinical: In children, fractures involving the epiphyseal plate (Salter–Harris) can disturb growth and cause a difference in limb length.
In osteoporosis bone mass and trabecular structure are reduced; fractures are most common in the vertebral bodies, the femoral neck and the distal radius.
Fracture healing passes through haematoma → soft callus (fibrocartilage) → hard callus (woven bone) → remodelling (lamellar bone).
tus: The clavicle is the first bone in the body to begin ossifying (weeks 5–6) and is mostly formed by intramembranous ossification.
Volkmann's canals run at right angles and connect the Haversian canals with each other and with the periosteum.

entries.summary: Small bones that develop within a tendon; they let the tendon glide over a bony prominence, reduce friction and increase the muscle's lever arm. The largest is the patella.
facts: Patella (quadriceps femoris tendon), pisiform (flexor carpi ulnaris tendon), the sesamoids under the MP joints of the thumb and the big toe
Protects the tendon, changes its direction and lengthens the lever arm, increasing the muscle's force
The fabella (in the lateral head of gastrocnemius) and the os peroneum (in the fibularis longus tendon) are present in some people
clinical: Inflammation of the sesamoids of the big toe (sesamoiditis) causes forefoot pain in dancers and runners.
The fabella and os peroneum can be mistaken for fracture fragments on X-ray.
tus: The patella is the largest sesamoid bone of the body; the pisiform is also regarded as a sesamoid developed in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris.
